title: How mechanical advantage works: levers, wedges, and inclined planes
mechanism_check: Every stuck thing or heavy lift is a force problem: identify the pivot (fulcrum), the load, and where you apply effort.
A lever multiplies force by the ratio of effort-arm to load-arm; a wedge multiplies by thinness; a screw is an inclined plane wrapped around a shaft.
improvised_tools: Any rigid bar (2x4, pipe, tire iron) as a lever; a block of wood as the fulcrum.
Door shims, chisels, or an axe head as wedges; soapy water to reduce friction on the plane.
steps: Find the pivot point closest to the load — that maximizes your effort arm.
Place the fulcrum on solid ground, never on the thing you're prying against if it can break.
Apply force gradually; if the lever flexes instead of the load moving, shorten the load arm.
For wedges: drive thin wedges in sequence rather than one thick wedge.
stop_conditions: The lever starts bending or the fulcrum crushes: your force exceeds the tool — stop and get a bigger lever.
The load shifts unpredictably: stop, re-seat, and keep body parts out of the crush zone.

title: Materials: what wood, metal, and plastic do under load
mechanism_check: Wood is strong along the grain, weak across it; it splits rather than bends past its limit.
Metal bends before it breaks (ductile) until work-hardened; plastic creeps under sustained load and softens with heat.
Match the material to the job: compression, tension, or bending — each wants a different material and section.
improvised_tools: No tools needed: this is knowledge. Test scraps by bending — feel where each material yields.
A magnet distinguishes steel from aluminum; a fingernail test tells softwood from hardwood.
steps: Identify the load direction on the part: bending, pulling, or crushing.
Choose grain direction (wood) or section shape (metal tube beats flat bar in bending).
Leave margin: improvised builds get chunkier sections than engineered ones.
Protect weak points: end grain, notches, and holes concentrate stress.
stop_conditions: Material cracking, crazing, or permanently deforming under test load: the section is too light — upsize it.
Unknown plastic under heat or load: stop — some plastics fail suddenly and some off-gas when heated.

title: Fasteners and joining: how threads, friction, and glue hold things
mechanism_check: Threads convert rotation into clamping force; the friction in the threads is what keeps them from backing out.
Glue joints are strongest in shear over large areas, weakest in peel; mechanical fasteners concentrate load at points.
A joint fails at its weakest element: the fastener, the substrate, or the interface.
improvised_tools: No tools needed: this is knowledge. Keep a screw assortment sorted by pattern and size.
Glue + clamp beats screws alone in wood; screws + glue beats either.
steps: For wood: glue the faces, clamp, then screw — the screws are the clamp until the glue cures.
For metal: match thread pitch exactly; a near-match strips under load.
Pre-drill pilot holes in wood near edges to prevent splitting.
Tighten in sequence (star pattern on multi-bolt joints) so clamping is even.
stop_conditions: Substrate crumbling around the fastener: the joint design is wrong — through-bolt with washers instead.
Glue joint starved (squeezed dry) or end-grain to end-grain: it will fail — redesign the joint.

title: Measure twice: layout, marking, and working to tolerance
mechanism_check: Every cut is a decision: mark the waste side with an X so the blade never eats the keep side.
Tolerance is how wrong you're allowed to be: framing tolerates 1/8 inch, joinery wants 1/32.
Measure from the same reference edge every time — switching references stacks error.
improvised_tools: A story stick (scrap marked with all positions) beats re-measuring.
A sharp pencil or knife line; a combination square or any true right angle.
The 3-4-5 triangle (or any multiple) lays out square corners with just a tape.
steps: Mark all positions from one reference edge before cutting anything.
Mark the waste side with an X on every cut line.
Cut proud of the line, then sneak up on it — you can't add wood back.
Dry-fit before glue or fasteners; check square with the 3-4-5 method.
stop_conditions: Measurements disagreeing by more than your tolerance: stop and find the bad reference before cutting.
Working without a square reference on joinery: stop — eyeballing compounds into a wracked assembly.

title: Cutting and shaping: saws, blades, and abrasives
mechanism_check: Saws cut on a stroke direction (most Western saws cut on push); the teeth set determines the kerf width.
Abrasives cut with grit: coarse shapes, fine finishes — skipping grits leaves scratches you can't polish out.
Blade choice is the cut: more teeth = smoother, fewer teeth = faster in thick stock.
improvised_tools: A sharp handsaw + clamped straightedge as a guide; sandpaper wrapped on a block.
A file for metal; a hacksaw with the right TPI (fine for thin stock, coarse for thick).
steps: Clamp the work and the guide — freehand starts straight and ends wavy.
Score the cut line with a knife first to prevent tear-out.
Let the tool do the work: steady rhythm, no forcing; forcing binds blades.
Work through grits in order (e.g. 80-120-220) when sanding to a finish.
stop_conditions: Blade binding, smoking, or wandering: stop — the work shifted or the blade is dull/wrong.
Cutting toward your body or bracing work with your hand in the blade path: stop and re-clamp.

title: Safety doctrine: eyes, lungs, hands, and stored energy
mechanism_check: Every job has stored energy: spring tension, pressurized lines, gravity-held loads, electrical charge, heat.
Name the energy before you start: what moves, what burns, what shocks, what falls if this lets go?
Dust and fumes are cumulative: one exposure is nothing, a habit is damage.
improvised_tools: Eye protection (even sunglasses beat nothing against chips); a dust mask or damp bandana.
Gloves matched to the hazard (cut vs chemical vs heat — one glove doesn't do all).
A fire extinguisher or water bucket within reach when heat or sparks are involved.
steps: Walk the job: list every energy source and how you'll release or avoid each.
De-energize: unplug it, shut the valve, bleed the pressure, chock the load.
Protect eyes and lungs first — they're the hardest to repair.
Keep a clear exit path; never position yourself where a slip drives you into the hazard.
stop_conditions: An energy source you can't identify or de-energize: stop — that's the job telling you it's out of scope.
Safety gear missing for an irreversible hazard (eyes, breathing): stop until you have it.

title: How water moves: pressure, flow, and seals
mechanism_check: Water moves from high pressure to low; flow is limited by the narrowest restriction.
Seals work by compression: O-rings, washers, and packing all need squeeze to seal.
Threads don't seal water — the washer, tape, or dope on them does.
improvised_tools: No tools needed: this is knowledge. A bucket and a watch measure flow rate.
PTFE tape (3 wraps, clockwise viewed from the pipe end) for threaded joints.
steps: Diagnose pressure vs flow: weak everywhere = pressure; weak at one fixture = local restriction.
Find the narrowest point: aerators, valves, and elbows are the usual suspects.
Seal threaded joints with tape/dope on the male threads; tighten to compress the seal.
Test under full pressure and watch every joint for 10 minutes.
stop_conditions: Pressure over ~80 psi at the house: the regulator has failed — fixtures will keep failing until it's replaced.
Water where it shouldn't be inside walls: stop diagnosing and shut the main — hidden leaks rot structure.

title: How electricity behaves: circuits, load, and why breakers trip
mechanism_check: Electricity needs a complete loop (circuit); current follows all paths, most through the least resistance.
Breakers trip from overcurrent (too much load) or faults (short/ground) — the trip is the protection working.
Wire gauge sets the safe current; the breaker protects the wire, not your devices.
improvised_tools: No tools needed: this is knowledge. A plug-in lamp is the simplest circuit tester.
The breaker panel directory (or making one) maps every circuit before you need it.
steps: Map which breaker feeds which outlets before doing any electrical work.
Add up loads on a circuit: watts / volts = amps; stay under 80% of the breaker rating.
A tripping breaker is a message: reduce load or find the fault — never upsize the breaker.
Test dead with a known-good lamp before touching anything.
stop_conditions: Burning smell, scorch marks, or a buzzing panel: stop and call an electrician — that's fault territory.
Anything inside the breaker panel or meter base: stop — that work is never DIY.

title: Friction, torque, and why stuck things stick
mechanism_check: Stuck threads are locked by corrosion (expanded rust in the valleys), threadlocker, or galling (metal welded by friction).
Torque is force times distance — a longer handle beats a stronger arm.
Shock breaks static friction better than steady force: impact > pull.
improvised_tools: Penetrating oil (capillary action carries it into threads); heat for differential expansion.
A cheater pipe over the wrench handle for leverage; hammer taps for shock.
A 6-point socket over a 12-point: more contact, less rounding.
steps: Identify the lock: rust (oil + shock), threadlocker (heat), galling (back off at the first squeal).
Soak with penetrating oil and tap the flats to help it creep.
Heat the outer (female) part to expand it away from the male thread.
Apply torque with the longest handle that fits; work back-and-forth in small arcs.
stop_conditions: The fastener or the part starts deforming: your torque exceeds the assembly — stop before it shears.
Heat near fuel, gas, or batteries: stop — pick a non-heat method.

title: Diagnosis before tools: the Sidewinder method
mechanism_check: Every fix starts with the same question: how is this held, fastened, or sealed? The answer picks the tool.
Symptoms lie upstream: a dead outlet may be a tripped breaker three rooms away.
List what you know, what you assume, and what one test would prove.
improvised_tools: Your eyes and hands first: look, wiggle, listen before reaching for anything.
One cheap test beats ten theories: the chalk mark, the tap test, the swap test.
steps: State the symptom in one sentence, then name the mechanism that could cause it.
Run the cheapest test that rules something out.
Match the tool to the mechanism — the right tool is a pattern (grip, torque, bite, heat, wedge), not a product.
Name the stop condition before you start: what breaks if you force it?
stop_conditions: Diagnosis keeps changing with each new symptom: stop — you're guessing; step back and re-observe.
The stop condition involves safety or structure you can't verify: stop and get eyes on it.
